title: Most-shared articles across regions
description: Aggregate the N most-shared articles globally in near-real time over the last five minutes, one hour, and one day, with 1M–10M distinct shared articles per day.
focus: asynchronous multi-region collection, article identity, three rolling windows, expiration without new events, safe Top-N merging, and snapshot serving.

children.value: Senior SWE / IC3 architecture field guide

Find the most-shared articles globally over the last five minutes, one hour, and one day. Start at the successful-share path; explain partitioned counting, time-driven expiration, and fast reads from complete snapshots.
Requirements → core entities → API → data flow → HLD → deep dives. One defensible design, not the only correct answer or a claim about production LinkedIn.
Trending means most shared, in three recent windows

LinkedIn allows users to share articles from 3rd party sites with their connections. Assume all share actions go through a common code path on the LinkedIn site (served by multiple servers in geographically diverse regions). Design a system to aggregate, in near-real time, the N most shared articles over the last five minutes, last hour and last day. Assume the number of unique shared articles per day is between 1M and 10M.
global frequency ranking of article shares
. It is not personalized feed ranking, stock-market shares, or automatically a velocity/growth score. The word
is defined by the prompt: most shares in a specified recent interval.
One existing share code path, many servers and regions
How a successful share is recorded; whether an event log or transactional outbox already exists.
Sliding boundaries, acceptable freshness, count precision, and the maximum N.
Total shares/day, peak shares/s, reads/s, URL sizes, and concentration on viral articles.
A quantitative freshness target; overnight batch processing cannot satisfy the five-minute use case.

Small example to confirm the meaning

If article A receives four shares in region East and four in region West, its global count is eight. An article with six shares entirely in East ranks below A, even though it wins within East. The five-minute winner can differ from the day's winner.

“I'll instrument the successful-share path, deliver events asynchronously, combine all regions' contributions by article, and maintain three rolling counters and rankings. Reads will fetch published results rather than recompute them.”
Agree on identity, time, and what can be approximate
Successful actions, attempts, unique sharers, and reshares produce different counts.
One count per successful eligible share action. A transport retry is not another share.
Tracking parameters, redirects, and URL aliases can split one article into multiple keys.
Use the site's canonical article ID and a versioned URL-normalization policy.
Local rankings cannot simply be concatenated into an exact global ranking.
Global across all configured contributing regions. Regional rankings are an extension.
Short buckets cost state; waiting for late events costs latency.
Propose a snapshot every 10 seconds, healthy-path cutoff age below 40 seconds, and P99 read latency below 100ms. These are targets to negotiate and measure.
Sampling, late-event rejection, and missing regions affect both counts and ordering.
Exact counters over admitted events at a declared 10-second-aligned cutoff; no sampling in the base design. Explicit lateness policy below.
The source explicitly permits discussing reliability versus performance.
Prefer existing durable share/outbox capture when available. A best-effort emitter is a legitimate alternative only with an agreed and monitored loss budget.
Bounds candidate merging, snapshot storage, and response size.
Propose 1–100; return fewer if fewer articles have positive counts.
What happens during a region outage?
A missing region can contain the true winner.
Serve the last globally complete snapshot with its original cutoff for an agreed bounded interval, then explicitly report unavailability. Do not disguise partial data as global.
is the age of the published cutoff.
concerns contributing regions and the admitted input. Exact counts at an older cutoff do not mean an exact answer for the wall-clock instant of the request.
For cutoff T and duration W, count events in

. All three windows share T. The left endpoint is included; the right endpoint is excluded. If exact arbitrary-instant boundaries are required, retain finer boundary information instead of claiming coarse buckets provide it.

Build capture, aggregation, ranking, and serving. Reuse the existing sharing service and article catalog; do not redesign the whole feed or social graph. Count only content eligible for a global trending surface. Personalized/private sharing, abuse scoring, unique-sharer counting, and arbitrary historical windows need explicit extensions.

one contribution per admitted event; all contributions for an article reach one logical count owner; expiration happens without new traffic; candidate truncation follows complete article aggregation; one publication uses one cutoff, policy version, and partition set.

“I'll first make the system work on one counting owner, then partition article identities. The important part is not naming Kafka and Redis; it is explaining what each one stores, how the window advances, and what happens when a worker or region disappears.”
Ten million URLs is a cardinality bound, not a QPS estimate
The source gives U = 1M–10M distinct articles/day. For a concrete sizing discussion,
100M shares/day, a 20× peak/average factor, 100-byte event payloads, and 10K ranking reads/s. The interviewer may replace all four numbers. Use decimal units below.
Two days, three replicas = 60 GB for one log tier, before overhead
Source-region logs plus the global log are separate copies, not included in that one-tier figure
Already material, before keys, ranks, maps, deduplication, or replicas. Exact only at matching bucket boundaries.
Blindly increasing resolution makes dense per-article rings expensive.
H ≤ admitted events/day. If H=100M and a packed row is 16 bytes: 1.6 GB of raw rows.
Indexing, bucket headers, allocation, and lateness headroom add overhead. One daily-active article need not occupy every bucket.
IDs, maps, and three ordered rank entries cost more. Short-window active sets may be much smaller than U.
A deliberately conservative case where every article is active in all windows; measure actual structure overhead.
100M IDs × 16 bytes = 1.6 GB of IDs alone for one day.
Expiry/index overhead is extra. Durable producer-sequence schemes can reduce this, but need a proof that retries retain their identity.
Why the serving path can remain small
Example logical partition count P = 64; N_max = 100
Three windows × 64 × 100 = 19,200 candidate rows per generation
At 64 bytes/row: 1.2288 MB every 10 seconds ≈ 122.88 KB/s
One all-window response: 3 × 100 × 64 = 19.2 KB before metadata/framing
At 10K reads/s: 192 MB/s of payload egress; use replicated regional serving

Possibly at the low end and with a compact layout. Cardinality alone does not prove a machine or database will fail. Include peak updates, indexing cost, allocation overhead, recovery time, and headroom. Partition when those measurements demand it; logical partitions are not a mandate for 64 physical machines.
Separate article identity, share events, rolling state, and results
Existing catalog. Do not store a long URL inside every counter or message if a stable ID is available.
Created by the successful-share path. Stable event_id survives CDC, relay, and consumer retries.
Sparse counts for ten-second event-time slices. The owner is determined by article_id, not geography.
Rolling sums derived from the retained buckets.
One ordered set per owner/window, containing all positive-count articles for that window.

Produced only after the owner has applied the agreed input frontier and expirations.

Removing a fragment may be safe under the site's policy; stripping arbitrary query parameters can merge different articles. Reuse canonicalization from the article subsystem. Redirect resolution and content fetching do not belong in the latency-sensitive counting path. A digest used for routing is not, by itself, proof that two URLs are identical.

The event needs no viewer identity for simple share counts. Restrict which events may enter this global aggregation, protect the underlying share log, and avoid exposing private article URLs through trending results.

07 · Derive each component from a bottleneck
Start with a working pipeline, then distribute the expensive part

The share service emits an event; one aggregator maintains article counters and ranks; a read endpoint returns the latest three lists. This establishes correctness and makes window expiration concrete. No request blocks on computing the ranking.
all ingestion, state, and recovery depend on one owner. A per-query scan of the entire day's events adds read amplification.
Stage 2: durable transport and precomputed serving

Introduce regional logs, replayable global ingestion, periodic counter snapshots, and a separate serving store. Readers do not touch hot counter state. The normal share write path remains isolated from aggregation lag.
transport decoupling alone has not increased counting capacity; one worker still owns every article.
Stage 3: partition by article, then merge small candidate sets

Route all occurrences of article X from every region to one logical owner. Owners count and rank in parallel. Each reports Top-N for each window at a common cutoff; a merger reads only those small lists.
truncation happens after each article has its complete global count. Partitioning the input by source host or region and truncating there would lose candidates.
This is incremental processing, not a new MapReduce job for every read. Batch jobs remain useful for reconciliation, backfills, and a slower day-level alternative if that product contract is relaxed.
Never make a user's share wait for the aggregation tier

reuse a source-local share transaction with a transactional outbox when available. The source datastore commits the share and its event record together. CDC or an outbox relay then publishes to a regional Kafka topic asynchronously. This adds no synchronous call to a global aggregator or another region.

If the existing site already has a durable successful-share event log, consume it instead of creating a second capture pipeline. If it has neither, an asynchronous buffered emitter may be the simpler answer: the source explicitly allows some data loss. State the loss/durability trade-off rather than pretending an in-process queue survives a crash.
Partitioned append-only logs, producer batching, retention/replay, and independent consumer groups suit a continuous aggregation workload. Existing operational expertise is a valid deciding factor.

Within the aggregation consumer group, each partition is processed by one active owner. Separate groups can consume the same events for audit, backfill, and abuse processing without stealing them from aggregation.
Producers publish batches; consumers pull according to their capacity. Consumer lag and retained logs make backpressure visible instead of turning it into synchronous share latency.

Replicated acknowledgments and outbox persistence improve recoverability but add storage/write overhead. Best-effort capture trades some accuracy for lower cost; choose with the interviewer, not silently.
Why not a blocking HTTP counter call?
It couples share availability and latency to the aggregator and the inter-region network. A slow counter should not prevent a member sharing an article.
Duplicates are a different problem from data loss
A relay can publish, lose the acknowledgment, and publish again. Preserve the original

; the owner deduplicates before adding to a bucket. Broker producer idempotence helps only within its documented producer/session scope; it does not automatically make CDC, cross-region relays, and restored state exactly-once end to end.

Deduplication state and consumed offsets must be included in the same consistent recovery checkpoint as counts. Retain dedup information for every event that can still affect an active window, plus allowed lateness and recovery margin. Older replays must be rejected by the event-time horizon rather than re-added after their dedup record expires.
Monitor captured-share versus event counts, outbox backlog, broker lag, retries, duplicates, and rejected timestamps. A best-effort alternative needs these loss metrics even more, not less.
09 · Partition the state, not the meaning of a count
All regions' shares of the same article reach the same owner
Regional relays forward events into a global topic partitioned by

. A logical article owner maintains complete counts for its subset of articles across East, West, and every other configured region. A consumer rebalance changes the active process, not the logical identity of the article's state.
Why “Top-N per region” is not enough

If each region sends only Top-1, X is missing from both lists and cannot win downstream. Sending every region's nonzero article count is lossless; sending only regional winners is not. A small regional rank error can become a large global error.

After shuffling by article, each article appears in exactly one owner's ranking with its complete global count. If X is not in that owner's Top-N, at least N articles on that owner precede X under the same total tie order. Those N also precede X globally. Therefore X cannot be in global Top-N. Apply this argument separately to the five-minute, hour, and day rankings.

All candidates must use the same cutoff T, ranking/filter policy, tie-break rule, and complete partition generation. Counts must be globally complete for each article. Increasing every local shortlist by an arbitrary factor does not repair a proof that lacks these conditions.
First exploit normal message batching. If one viral article saturates its owner, aggregate

counts for that article per region/ten-second bucket, with retry-stable contribution IDs, or introduce salted partial counters and a second sum stage. Combine those partials into one complete article total before ranking; never rank salted fragments as different articles.
One sparse history; three independently expiring totals

counts, where b is the bucket start. A five-minute window spans 30 buckets; one hour spans 360; one day spans 8,640. The history is shared; an article also has three current totals and corresponding rank entries.
C_W(article, T) = sum B[b][article] for T-W <= b < T
C_W(article, T+delta) = C_W(article, T) + B[T][article] - B[T-W][article]
W in {300s, 3600s, 86400s}; T and W align to delta
according to the agreed source-progress/lateness frontier.
For each of the three windows, apply incoming article counts and subtract that window's outgoing bucket. Update only affected articles.
For every changed total, remove its old ordered rank entry and insert the new positive-count entry. A zero total has no entry in that window.
Record the new cutoff and emit owner-local candidates. Drive this with recoverable progress/timers even if the incoming bucket is empty.
Reclaim history only after it is no longer needed by the day window or the recovery/lateness policy. Do not delete a five-minute-expired bucket while the hour/day windows still need it.

At owner p, advancing from T to T + delta:
    for W in {5m, 1h, 1d}:
        changes = incoming B[T] minus outgoing B[T-W]
        for each changed article:
            old = totals[W][article]
            new = old + changes[article]
            remove (old, article) from rank[W] if old > 0
            store new and insert (new, article) if new > 0
    persist cutoff = T + delta

This is algorithmic pseudocode for a design interview, not an incomplete Coding 2 solution. In production, counters, rank state, cutoff, and consumed offsets must move through a consistent state transition/checkpoint. Negative totals signal a duplicate/expiration bug; do not clamp them to zero and hide it.
The source's five-minute buckets need a boundary contract
The source suggests 288 five-minute buckets per URL. That supports exact five-minute-aligned lookbacks. It does

reconstruct a literal rolling five-minute window ending at an arbitrary instant. At 12:05:01, a share from 12:04:59 still belongs in the last five minutes, although the current calendar bucket started at 12:05:00.

Our ten-second buckets are still a negotiated resolution, not magic. They give exact interval membership at ten-second-aligned cutoffs. If exact second-level or arbitrary-instant answers matter, use finer buckets or retain timestamped boundary events; recompute ranking against the corrected counts, not just against an old shortlist.

Budget up to 20 seconds for out-of-order arrival, 10 seconds for the publication cadence, and 10 seconds for processing/publication: a proposed 40-second cutoff-age target. A watermark is derived from actual source progress and the lateness allowance, not blindly from the wall clock. Delayed relays hold it back; quiet partitions need trustworthy progress/heartbeat information so their empty windows can advance.

For the base immutable-snapshot policy, an event arriving behind the finalized frontier is excluded from the live ranking, counted in lateness metrics, and retained for offline reconciliation. Do not silently rewrite an already published snapshot. If the product needs corrections, introduce explicit revised generations. Validate implausible future timestamps instead of letting one advance the watermark past valid events.
11 · A result heap is not the whole algorithm
Keep every active candidate, not just today's winners
At each owner, maintain an ordered index for each window keyed by
. This can be a balanced tree alongside a hash map of counts, or an equivalent ordered state structure. It supports both increments and expiration-driven decrements in
time, and reading the first N entries in
Why not store only N articles?

If article A's old shares expire, article B can become the winner without a new B share arriving. B must still be represented somewhere searchable. Exact ranking cannot discard every nonwinner just because the output is small.
Keep totals and periodically scan all active articles into a size-N heap for each window: roughly O(U log N) per publication. Easy to reason about; benchmark against the 10-second budget.
Maintain all positive totals in ordered per-window indexes. Update affected entries as buckets enter/leave, then read Top-N without rescanning every article.

Do not call a sorted-set update O(1), confuse a max-heap's internal array with a sorted list, or claim a tiny Top-N heap eliminates the O(U) state behind exact results. Candidate merging at the publisher is cheap precisely because expensive article-level counting was already distributed.
The publisher can merge P sorted candidate lists with a heap in roughly
work per window once it has their heads; transporting all P×N candidates remains bounded. Reusing stable snapshot payloads across all readers avoids redoing this per query.
Publish complete generations and serve them cheaply
Owners emit their three candidate lists under
. Empty lists are still explicit completion records.
The merger waits for the expected partition manifest for that epoch. A timeout does not transform a partial set into a complete result.
Merge each window independently using the same tie order. Write an immutable payload with all three lists and coverage metadata.
After the payload is durable, atomically publish its manifest pointer. Readers fetch the pointer once and then that immutable generation, preventing mixed-window responses.
Replicate snapshots to regional serving caches/KV stores. Trending API replicas serve without contacting every source machine or counter owner.

Use a single fenced publisher or conditional generation updates so an old publisher cannot move the manifest backward. A cache miss loads the latest durable published snapshot, not a fresh scan of share history. Coalesce concurrent cache refreshes and retain the previous complete payload during replacement.

Article titles/thumbnails are optional enrichment from the catalog. Rank article IDs first and batch-enrich only the returned IDs. A slow metadata fetch should not stall aggregation. Apply removal/visibility controls in serving as well; if filtering removes winners, returning fewer is safer than leaking content. Exact replacement winners require updated eligible ranks or a proven refill strategy, not an arbitrary fixed overfetch.
13 · Answer the source's storage questions directly
What must survive, and what can be rebuilt?
The business action survives independently of trending computation.
Replay after worker or relay failure. Retention must cover checkpoint age, replay needs, and the oldest required window.
Restore consistently with source offsets; rank indexes may be rebuilt from totals if that recovery cost is acceptable.
Includes routing/ownership epoch and cutoff. Restoring counters without expiry position is incomplete.
Replicated KV/object payloads plus regional caches
Preserve the last complete result while computation catches up.
Not necessarily for every mutable counter.

If losing a day's trend history during a correlated failure is acceptable, redundant in-memory owners may be enough. If fast recovery and avoiding a cold day-window restart matter, keep replayable input and checkpoints. Replication protects selected failures; it does not automatically protect against deletion bugs, correlated loss, or expired logs.

The source suggests Redis. It can host partitioned counts/ranks or small serving snapshots, but saying “Redis” does not define expiration, atomic updates, replay, or failover. If counters and sorted ranks live there, group an article owner's state consistently, handle updates atomically within the supported shard boundary, and decide what persists. The base design can instead keep counters in a stream processor and use Redis only for serving caches.
Why not put every analytics operation in one database?

A single write-heavy event table plus repeated global grouping/ranking becomes a throughput, read-amplification, and failure bottleneck as volume rises. That is a workload argument, not proof that a named relational database cannot handle 1M distinct articles. A database is perfectly reasonable for the small published rankings or for a measured low-scale baseline.
Local capture, one logical global aggregation, regional reads

Each region writes its own share/outbox and replicated event log without a cross-region round trip in the user path. Asynchronous relays feed a global aggregation deployment, whose brokers/workers are replicated across failure domains. Its snapshots are served from regional replicas. There is one active logical owner per article partition; replicas are not independent contributions to the count.

transmit compact article IDs and batches; compress on the wire. The same logical event retains its ID across hops. If regional partial aggregation is added, transmit every nonzero article/bucket contribution and deduplicate contribution retries before summing.

Distinguish a regional serving-cache failure from missing input. A cache can fail over to another copy of the same published generation. If a source region's relay stops, global input coverage and the common watermark may stop advancing. Serve the old snapshot with its real age, or adopt an explicit partial-results policy if availability is more important than globally complete ranking.

After a delay longer than retention, rebuilding the affected state may require a retained checkpoint or a source backfill. Do not replay both primary and mirror events as separate shares. If the global compute region fails, promote a standby with fencing, restore a consistent epoch, and resume from known input positions before publishing again.
A real trade-off, not a slogan

You cannot promise always-fresh, complete global rankings while one contributing region is unreachable. The source permits some data loss; that makes an availability-oriented partial/approximate policy negotiable, not invisible.
Share commits; process crashes before export
The share disappears from trending if it lived only in memory.
Outbox/CDC resumes after restart. For best-effort capture, count this against the agreed loss budget.
Stable event IDs and owner-side dedup; do not mint a new ID on each relay attempt.
Worker dies between count and rank updates
Rank and totals disagree, or expiration is repeated.
Restore consistent checkpointed state and offsets, replay deterministically, and publish only recovered complete cutoffs.
Recoverable time/progress advancement expires buckets independently of arrivals.
One owner is late at publication
Its article might be the missing global winner.
Keep the last complete snapshot; alert on owner/region lag rather than silently merge only responders.
Two workers think they own one partition
Ownership epochs, fencing, and expected-partition manifests.
An incomplete or unreachable payload is advertised.
Immutable payload first, manifest last; unreferenced payload can be safely reclaimed later.
Future timestamps can distort windows or force bad watermark advancement.
Validate trusted source timestamps, quarantine anomalies, and expose error metrics.
One owner falls behind, affecting global freshness.
Measure per-key skew; batch, add partial-count stages if needed, and preserve complete counts before ranking.

Extend the architecture without breaking its invariants
Could Hadoop or a warehouse solve this?

The source notes that a day-lookback batch job may be reasonable, but a five-minute near-real-time result is unlikely to tolerate a large batch pipeline's delay. Keep the streaming path for fresh rankings. Use batch for reconciliation or a separately agreed slower day result; do not claim an overnight batch meets the same freshness contract.
What if a little inaccuracy is acceptable?

Agree whether the relaxation covers lost events, approximate counts, approximate Top-N membership, or temporal resolution. Sampling and sketches require a candidate-discovery mechanism and aging strategy; an insertion-only lifetime sketch is not a rolling-window ranking. Quantify error and measure close-rank instability. Avoid buying formal exactness the product does not need.
What if the top article gets most of the traffic?

Batch first. If needed, combine source/region counts per article and bucket, using retry-stable batch identity, or salt partial counters and reduce them again by article. Keep all partial counts; the final rank stage must see the complete article total. Adding partitions alone does not split a single hot key.
What if the question really means growth rate or momentum?

That changes the score. Define a formula using recent and baseline rates, treatment of newly seen articles, smoothing, and minimum support. Raw count Top-N cannot answer that by itself. The source prompt specifies most-shared articles, so do not silently introduce a decay or velocity score.
What if we count unique sharers, not share actions?

A counter is no longer enough. Track membership per article/window or an approximate distinct-count structure with explicit window expiration and identity/privacy rules. Regional distinct counts cannot simply be summed if the same member can appear in more than one region.
What if a share or article is deleted?

First decide whether deleting a share retracts a historical count. If yes, retain enough event-to-bucket identity to apply a deduplicated retraction to every affected active window. Do not subtract the same event again on later expiry. Article takedown also needs immediate serving suppression, even while the counting pipeline catches up.
Can we return a personalized or regional Top-N?

Regional fixed aggregations can use a composite partitioning/grouping plan. Arbitrary per-viewer visibility or personalization is not just a parameter on global snapshots: the global winners may all be ineligible for a viewer. State the new candidate, privacy, and fan-out cost before promising the same read latency.
Could we only keep the three current totals?

No: totals alone do not tell us how much to subtract as events age out. Retain time-indexed contributions, an expiration schedule, or an equivalent replayable history. Three independent timers on whole-article totals are incorrect when that article has activity at many times.
Could one global Redis sorted set handle everything?

Maybe at a measured small scale, but it centralizes write load and failure. Three sorted sets still need correct per-window decrements, replay, and atomic count/rank updates. For scale, partition full article counts, then merge complete-owner candidates.
A senior-level narrative, in dependency order

“We need global Top-N articles by successful share count over trailing five minutes, one hour, and one day. I'll clarify canonical article identity, N, freshness, and acceptable loss. Ten million distinct articles tells me state size, not the number of updates per second.”

“The common share path is the capture point. I will deliver events asynchronously to a counter service, compute the three lists once, and expose them through a read API. The user request must not wait for aggregation in another region.”

“Kafka gives us batching, partitions, independent consumers, and replay. If the existing share transaction supports an outbox, I reuse it; if the product accepts loss and has no durable capture path, a buffered emitter is cheaper, with explicit loss monitoring.”

“All regions' events for article A go to one logical owner. I do not send only each region's Top-N, because an article can lose locally everywhere but win globally. Once each owner's counts are complete, local Top-N merging is safe.”

“Each owner keeps sparse ten-second counts and three rolling sums. Every cutoff adds the incoming bucket and subtracts a different outgoing bucket for five minutes, one hour, and one day. That happens even with no new shares. An ordered index retains all active candidates so yesterday's loser can become today's winner after expiration.”
6. Make the read and failure paths explicit

“I publish one immutable three-window snapshot only after all expected owners reach the same cutoff. Regional APIs read that version cheaply. If a region or owner is late, I serve the last complete version with its original age, rather than publish a partial result as fresh global truth.”

“The main costs are article-time state, rank maintenance, and cross-region input. Ten-second cutoffs and the lateness policy trade a little freshness for bounded work. If that precision is unnecessary, we can reduce capture/state cost; if strict arbitrary-instant exactness is necessary, we need more boundary data.”

A poor candidate will have difficulty decomposing the problem into a reasonable architecture.
A good candidate will easily decompose the problem into a set of reasonable set of services.
A great candidate will ask probe the interviewer about data rates and sizes, single vs multi-colo requirements, etc.
Source: evaluation paragraph under Aggregation Service
A poor candidate will suggest issuing a blocking call back to the aggregation tier while processing share events.
A good candidate will propose a messaging system to deliver the share event to the aggregation tier.
A great candidate will have a sound recommendation for a specific messaging system based on experience and will be able to defend their choice.
The page also calls out persistent-storage necessity, partitioning, and the risk of a single database instance. It does
supply a complete numeric scorecard, an interview time limit, mandatory technologies, or an explicit “AE requires X” rule. The table below is our preparation coverage, not additional quoted criteria.
Existing share tier, transport, aggregation, and data store, connected end to end.
Separate share rate, distinct articles, per-bucket state, peak load, and read egress.
Local capture, asynchronous replication, global count ownership, and degraded behavior.
Point-to-point versus pub/sub, push/pull, reliability versus performance.
Three lookbacks, bucket sizing, no-arrival expiration, and separate rankings.
Complete counts per article; safe Top-N merge after that reduction.
Distinguish redundant mutable state from replay/checkpoints; tie durability to product tolerance.
Study notes: useful source hints that need qualification
a useful five-minute-resolution starting point, not arbitrary-instant exact sliding windows.
Evict URLs when a new URL arrives:
not enough on its own; time advances during silence too, and short-window counts must expire before day-level eviction.
true only for the failure/loss/rebuild budget you accepted; simultaneous loss still matters.
One named database will fall over:
explain measured workload bottlenecks rather than asserting a product cannot handle an unspecified write rate.
